questions.q: What is an OpenAPI document?
questions.explain: It answers the questions every API user asks: which paths exist, what do I send, what comes back, which errors can happen. Because it is plain JSON or YAML, both people and programs can read it.
options: A program that runs your API in the cloud
A JSON or YAML file that describes every path, method, input and response of an HTTP API
A database schema for the API's tables
A test suite for HTTP routes

questions.q: Which of these is not something the lesson says tools do with an OpenAPI document?
questions.explain: The document only describes the API. It protects nothing. Authentication still has to be enforced by your server on every route.
options: Show browsable documentation, such as Swagger UI or ReDoc
Generate a client library for your API in another language
Check in CI that the API did not change by accident
Enforce authentication on your routes at runtime

questions.q: Why does the lesson build the document with @zudojs/openapi instead of writing the file by hand?
questions.explain: When the document is built from the same schemas that validate requests, it cannot drift away from what the API really does.
options: Hand-written files are not valid OpenAPI
A hand-written file goes out of date the day the code changes; building it from your schemas and routes keeps them in step
The package makes the API faster
Swagger UI only reads generated files

questions.q: What are the three main parts of an OpenAPI document?
questions.explain: info holds the API's name and version, paths every URL and what each method does there, and components the shared pieces, such as schemas.

questions.q: In OpenAPI, what is an operation?
questions.explain: GET /tasks/{id} and DELETE /tasks/{id} are two operations on the same path. Each has its own operationId, parameters and responses.
options: One method on one path, such as GET /tasks/{id}
A server that runs the API

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The router style :id becomes {id}, the way OpenAPI writes a path parameter. The keys of paths are URLs, not operation ids.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: OpenAPI demands required: true for every path parameter, so the manager adds it. A URL without the id would simply be a different path.

questions.q: What is operationId used for?
questions.explain: A generated client might offer tasks.get(...) for the operation with operationId: "tasks.get". It must be unique in the document.
options: It is the database id of the route
It is a unique name for the operation; client generators turn it into a method name
It sets the HTTP status code
It decides the order of routes

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: By default the manager adds the ZudoJS logo to info as x-logo, a field some viewers read. branding: false leaves it out and keeps the output short.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A reference is an object with a $ref that points into the document. An operation uses it to say "the body is a Task" without copying the whole schema.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: addSchema translates your schema into OpenAPI's schema language and stores it under components.schemas. .min(3).max(100) become minLength and maxLength, and title is required.

questions.q: The schema has no .max(). What does this print?
questions.explain: @zudojs/schema applies a limit of 255 characters to every string by default. The document tells clients the real limit, so they are not surprised by a 422.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: .int() becomes "type": "integer" and .min(1) becomes "minimum": 1. min includes the value itself, so it is not exclusive.

questions.q: What do addSecurityScheme("bearerAuth", { type: "http", scheme: "bearer" }) and addSecurityRequirement({ bearerAuth: [] }) do together?
questions.explain: The scheme says how callers prove who they are; the requirement says it applies everywhere. Both only describe the API. Your server still has to check the token.
options: They check the token on every request
They document that callers send a bearer token in the Authorization header, and make that the rule for every operation
They create a new token for each user
They hide every route from the docs

questions.q: What does security: [] on the /health operation mean?
questions.explain: An empty list overrides the document-wide requirement for that operation. It is right for a health check that load balancers call without a token.
options: No sign-in is needed for that one operation
The route is hidden from the docs

questions.q: When should you choose OpenAPI 3.0 instead of 3.1?
questions.explain: 3.1 is the current version and matches JSON Schema. Choose 3.1 unless a tool forces you to use 3.0. The manager writes the right keywords for whichever you pick.
options: Always, because it is older and more stable
Only when a tool you must support, such as an older code generator or gateway, reads only 3.0
When the API has more than 10 paths

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A value that may be null is written "nullable": true in 3.0 and as a list of types, ["string", "null"], in 3.1.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: gt(0) means "greater than 0, not equal". 3.1 writes "exclusiveMinimum": 0; 3.0 writes "minimum": 0 plus "exclusiveMinimum": true.

questions.q: Your openapi.json parses fine with JSON.parse. Is the document correct?
questions.explain: validate() checks the OpenAPI rules and returns { valid, errors, warnings }. Being valid JSON only means the brackets match.
options: Yes, valid JSON is a valid document
Not necessarily: it can still break OpenAPI rules, such as a $ref that points nowhere; check it with manager.validate()
Yes, if it has an info field

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The operation asks for a security scheme called bearer that the document never declares. Such a document looks protected, but tools cannot tell how to send a token. Declare it with addSecurityScheme.

questions.q: Why is an undeclared security scheme a real problem and not just a style issue?
questions.explain: A generated client would not know to add an Authorization header, and readers are misled about how to call the API. The validator catches it.
options: The document looks protected, but tools and client generators cannot tell how to send a token
It turns off authentication on the server

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The $ref points at a Task schema that was never added with addSchema. The validator follows every reference and reports the ones that go nowhere.
options: [ 'Schema "Task" is not a valid JSON Schema.' ]

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: generate(true) validates first and throws an OpenAPIValidationError when something is wrong. In a build script, that stops a broken document from being written.

questions.q: What does the lesson advise about the responses of each route?
questions.explain: Only you know what a route really answers: a DELETE that answers 204, a create that answers 201, the errors a client must handle. A document that guesses is a document that lies.
options: Leave them out; the manager fills them in correctly
Always write them yourself, including error responses like 401, 404 and 422

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: YAML writes the same data with indentation instead of braces. Nested fields such as title are indented under info:.
options:
openapi: 3.1.0
info:
  title: Task API
  version: 1.0.0

openapi: 3.1.0
info: { title: Task API, version: 1.0.0 }

- openapi: 3.1.0
- info:
  - title: Task API
  - version: 1.0.0

questions.q: Why does the build script call toJSON(true) and toYAML(true)?
questions.explain: Validating before saving means the committed files are always valid. If something is wrong, the script throws instead of writing a bad file.
options: true validates first, so a broken document is never written to disk

questions.q: Why commit openapi.yaml to git?
questions.explain: A diff in openapi.yaml is an easy-to-read summary of an API change. An accidental breaking change is spotted in review instead of by your users.
options: So the server can read it at startup
When someone changes a route or schema, the difference shows up in the review, and everybody sees how the API changed
Git needs it to build the project

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: toResponse() gives { status, headers, body } with the document as JSON text. It works with any HTTP server: you copy the status, headers and body into your response.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: toUIResponse gives a complete HTML page with Swagger UI, which loads the document from specUrl. It comes with a content security policy that only allows scripts from the pinned CDN and the page's own known inline script.

questions.q: The docs page loads Swagger UI from a CDN. How does the manager protect it if the CDN file is ever changed by an attacker?
questions.explain: An integrity hash is a fingerprint of the exact file. If one byte changes, the fingerprint does not match and the browser blocks the script. The CSP header also limits where scripts may come from.
options: It does not; CDN files are always safe
The scripts are pinned to exact versions with integrity hashes, so the browser refuses to run a changed file
It downloads the file once and stores it in the database
It asks the user to confirm before running scripts

questions.q: Which of these is safe to put in an operation's description or example?
questions.explain: Everything in the document is visible to anyone who can open /docs. Use made-up examples only, never secrets, internal hosts or real tokens.
options: A real bearer token, so readers can try the API
The internal host name of the database
A made-up example task such as { "title": "Buy milk" }
An admin password for the test server

questions.q: A route is marked hidden: true, so it is left out of the document. Is it protected?
questions.explain: Hiding a route from the docs is not security. Attackers guess paths, read old documents and front-end code. Every route needs its own authentication and permission checks.
options: Yes, because nobody knows it exists
No: an attacker can still call it; protect every route with authentication, documented or not
Yes, if the document is served over HTTPS

questions.q: In the last section, what does the loop over registry.getAll() give you?
questions.explain: The registry already knows each operation's name, input and output schemas, description and tags. Building the document from it means a new operation is documented the next time you build.
options: Every operation in the registry appears in the document automatically, with its schemas, description and tags; nothing to forget
A second copy of each operation for testing

questions.q: The check-docs.ts script finds problems. How does it make the CI job fail?
questions.explain: CI looks at the exit code, not at the text. A non-zero exit code fails the build, so a broken reference never reaches the people who use your API.
options: It prints the problems and sets process.exitCode = 1
It throws inside a try/catch that ignores the error

questions.q: Finish toOpenAPIPath(path): turn router parameters like :id into OpenAPI's {id}. The program should print /tasks/{id}/comments/{commentId} and then /health.
questions.explain: A regular expression with the g flag finds every :name, and {$1} puts the captured name inside braces. A path without parameters stays as it is.

questions.q: Finish pathParameters(path): return one OpenAPI parameter object for each {name} in an OpenAPI path, as { name, in: "path", required: true, schema: { type: "string" } }. The program should print the line in the comment.
questions.explain: matchAll finds every {…} and the capture group holds the name. Every path parameter must have required: true: OpenAPI demands it.

questions.q: Build an OpenAPI paths object by hand. Finish describeGet(path, operationId) so it returns { [path]: { get: { operationId, responses: { "200": { description: "OK" }, "404": { description: "Not found" } } } } }. The program should print the line in the comment.
questions.explain: A computed key, [path], uses the variable's value as the property name. Under the path sits the method, and under the method the operation with its id and responses. Status codes are string keys.

questions.q: Finish nullableString(maxLength, version) so it writes a nullable string the way each OpenAPI version expects: for "3.0.3" use "nullable": true; for "3.1.0" use a type list with "null". The program should print the two lines in the comments.
questions.explain: The same idea has two spellings. Mind the key order: JSON.stringify writes keys in the order you created them. In real code, pass version to the manager and let it choose.

questions.q: Write a tiny validator. Finish brokenRefs(document, refs): each ref looks like #/components/schemas/Task. Return the refs whose schema name is not a key of document.components.schemas. The program should print [ '#/components/schemas/NewTask' ].
questions.explain: Take the name after the prefix and check that the document really contains it. Object.hasOwn ignores inherited keys. This is one of the checks manager.validate() does for you.

questions.q: Finish unknownSchemes(requirements, schemes). requirements is an operation's security list, like [{ bearer: [] }]. Return the scheme names used there that are not keys of schemes. The program should print [ 'bearer' ] and then [].
questions.explain: Each requirement is an object whose keys are scheme names. flatMap collects them all, and the filter keeps the ones the document never declared. An empty list means every scheme is known.

questions.q: Document operations from a registry. Finish buildPaths(operations): for each operation, add a path /api/<name> with a post operation whose operationId is the name and whose tags come from the operation. The program should print the two lines in the comments.
questions.explain: One loop documents every operation, so adding an operation to the registry adds it to the document too. The real version also registers each input and output schema as a component.
